guides.title: Fine-tuning dataset design
guides.summary: Fine-tuning dataset design turns a measured behavior gap into representative training examples with clear labels, coverage and provenance while keeping evaluation cases separate enough to tell whether training actually generalized.
guides.mentalModel: Training data is a specification expressed through examples. Its distribution tells the model which behavior to reinforce, so dataset design should mirror the target gap without leaking the test that will later judge success.
guides.whyItMatters: Adapters and fine-tuning make optimization easy to start, but weak data can encode noise, shortcuts or historical mistakes. A smaller curated dataset that represents the failure modes often teaches more than a large dump of production logs and produces evidence that is easier to audit.

sections.title: Design from the target failure distribution
sections.body: Define the behavior to change and collect examples that cover common, difficult and boundary cases. Normalize labels and instructions, remove duplicates and leakage, track source and consent constraints, and split by meaningful units such as user, document or time when random row splits would leak near-duplicates. Hold out slices that represent the original failure so training and evaluation remain independent.

sections.title: Example: support fine-tune memorizes repeated ticket templates
sections.body: A team trains on thousands of historical tickets and reports near-perfect validation accuracy using a random split. Many tickets are near-duplicate templates, so the same patterns appear in train and test. Splitting by customer and time, deduplicating templates and curating hard escalation cases reveals a much smaller real gain and a clearer target for the adapter.

failureModes: Using raw production logs as training data without curation or provenance.
Randomly splitting near-duplicate examples and mistaking leakage for generalization.
Optimizing the dataset for average frequency while omitting costly boundary cases.
heuristics: Start from a measured behavior gap and design examples to cover it.
Split data on the unit that would create real-world leakage if shared.
Keep held-out failure slices outside the training loop until release evaluation.
takeaways: Fine-tuning data is an executable behavior specification.
Curation and split design determine whether evaluation is believable.
More examples do not compensate for leakage or missing failure coverage.

guides.title: Research to outline
guides.summary: Research-to-outline turns collected evidence into a structure of claims, questions and sections so long-form generation follows what the evidence can support instead of inventing a narrative first and searching for citations afterward.
guides.mentalModel: An outline is a claim architecture. Each section should have a purpose, supporting evidence and unresolved questions; prose comes later, after the evidence structure is coherent enough to guide drafting.
guides.whyItMatters: AI makes drafting cheap, which tempts writers to generate a polished structure before research has revealed what is true or important. Evidence-first outlining keeps the narrative flexible, exposes gaps early and reduces the risk of forcing sources into a preselected story.

sections.title: Build the outline from claim and evidence clusters
sections.body: Group research notes by the decisions or claims they can support, preserve disagreements, and identify which clusters deserve a section. For each section, record its question, provisional claim, strongest evidence and missing evidence. Order sections by reader dependency and argument flow, then allow the structure to change when new sources weaken or split a claim.

sections.title: Example: a market report is outlined before interviews are read
sections.body: An author asks an AI to create ten chapters from the project brief, then tries to fit interview evidence into those headings. Several findings contradict the original story. Rebuilding the outline around evidence clusters produces fewer sections, adds a disagreement section and marks one claim as unresolved instead of hiding the contradiction.

failureModes: Creating the final outline before reviewing the evidence landscape.
Using topic labels as sections without defining the claim or question each one resolves.
Discarding contradictory evidence because it disrupts a cleaner narrative.
heuristics: Give every section an evidence-backed purpose before drafting prose.
Keep unresolved questions visible in the outline instead of filling them with generated text.
Reorder or split sections when evidence structure changes.
takeaways: A strong outline is a map of supported claims, not a table of contents generated from keywords.
Evidence should shape narrative structure before prose generation.
Visible gaps in an outline are cheaper to fix than unsupported claims in a finished draft.

guides.title: Claim–evidence matrix
guides.summary: A claim–evidence matrix maps important conclusions to supporting and contradicting sources, provenance, freshness and confidence so research can be audited before it is compressed into a narrative.
guides.mentalModel: Treat every important claim as a row whose evidence must earn the right to appear. Sources are not decoration after writing; they are structured inputs that reveal support, disagreement and missing proof.
guides.whyItMatters: Research assistants can produce fluent synthesis while hiding weak provenance or combining sources that repeat the same underlying report. A matrix makes independence and conflict visible and gives reviewers a compact artifact for deciding which claims are ready, disputed or unsupported.

sections.title: Separate claims from the evidence that qualifies them
sections.body: Define candidate claims at the level a reader could challenge. For each, record supporting sources, contradicting sources, original provenance, date and notes on independence. Mark whether evidence is direct or inferred and whether the claim is ready, needs qualification or remains unresolved. Generate prose from the matrix only after the evidence state is explicit.

sections.title: Example: five articles appear to confirm one market number
sections.body: A research agent finds five articles quoting the same market-size figure and reports strong consensus. The matrix traces all five back to one vendor report, so independence is actually one. A second source gives a different estimate, and the final claim is written as a range with provenance rather than as falsely certain consensus.

failureModes: Counting syndicated or derivative sources as independent confirmation.
Storing citations without recording which exact claim each source supports.
Collapsing conflicting evidence into one average before a reviewer can see the disagreement.
heuristics: Track original provenance behind repeated coverage.
Require important claims to point to explicit supporting evidence rows.
Preserve contradiction and uncertainty as states in the matrix.
takeaways: Evidence quality depends on provenance and independence, not citation count.
A matrix exposes unsupported claims before narrative compression.
Research synthesis is stronger when disagreement remains inspectable.

guides.title: Media quality review
guides.summary: Media quality review evaluates generated images, audio, video and presentation assets against instructional purpose, factual accuracy, accessibility, brand constraints and technical delivery rather than accepting output because it looks polished.
guides.mentalModel: Generated media is a product artifact with a job to do. Review should ask whether the asset communicates the intended concept correctly and survives the real viewing or listening environment, not only whether it is aesthetically pleasing.
guides.whyItMatters: AI can create visually convincing media that contains wrong labels, unreadable text, inconsistent diagrams or accessibility failures. In educational products those errors can teach the wrong mental model. A review contract turns taste into inspectable acceptance criteria.

sections.title: Review meaning, usability and delivery separately
sections.body: Start from the learning objective and list the information the asset must convey. Check semantic correctness, hierarchy, legibility, captions or transcripts, color/contrast and device constraints. Then validate technical properties such as dimensions, duration, compression and file size. Keep a reject/revise reason so repeated generation failures become data for improving the production workflow.

sections.title: Example: beautiful diagram teaches the wrong data flow
sections.body: A generated architecture illustration is visually strong but places the verifier before the tool result, implying the system verifies intent rather than outcome. A semantic review catches the causal error, while a purely aesthetic review would approve it. The asset is regenerated with the correct flow and then tested at mobile size for label legibility.

failureModes: Approving generated media primarily on visual appeal.
Checking technical file properties while missing a wrong concept or label.
Treating accessibility fixes as optional polish after publication.
heuristics: Tie each asset to an explicit communication or learning objective.
Review semantic correctness before aesthetics and compression.
Test the final media in the actual device, caption and accessibility context.
takeaways: Polished media can still teach the wrong thing.
Quality review needs semantic, accessibility and technical gates.
Reject reasons should feed the next generation or editing step.

guides.title: Customer problem research
guides.summary: Customer problem research gathers evidence about recurring user pain, current workarounds, consequences and willingness to change before a solo builder automates or markets a solution.
guides.mentalModel: Treat a problem as an evidence-backed pattern, not an idea. The strongest signal is a repeated costly behavior or workaround tied to a specific context, not positive reactions to a proposed feature.
guides.whyItMatters: AI makes building fast, which increases the cost of solving the wrong problem at high speed. For solo operators, a few weeks spent automating low-value demand can consume the same scarce attention needed for acquisition and support. Problem research creates a decision gate before implementation.

sections.title: Collect behavior before asking for approval
sections.body: Define a narrow customer segment, interview or observe recent concrete situations, and capture trigger, current workaround, frequency, cost and consequence. Look for repeated patterns across independent users and test whether they will spend time, money or workflow change to solve the issue. Keep solution language out of early questions so evidence is not shaped by your own idea.

sections.title: Example: users praise an AI dashboard but keep using spreadsheets
sections.body: A founder interviews ten operators and shows an AI analytics concept. Everyone says it sounds useful, but follow-up questions reveal their real recurring pain is reconciling exports from two systems before weekly reporting. A small reconciliation workflow attracts immediate trial use, while the dashboard idea is deferred because enthusiasm did not map to behavior.

failureModes: Asking users whether they like the proposed solution instead of studying recent behavior.
Generalizing from one loud request without checking frequency across a segment.
Treating social engagement as equivalent to willingness to change workflow or pay.
heuristics: Ask about the last concrete occurrence of the problem, not hypothetical interest.
Record existing workaround, frequency and consequence for every interview.
Require behavioral evidence before committing scarce solo-builder capacity.
takeaways: Problem evidence should precede automation and growth effort.
Current workarounds reveal more than polite feature enthusiasm.
A narrow repeated pain is more actionable than a broad attractive idea.
